commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether an accountable, multidisciplinary AI governance body improves safety, equity, or performance of AI in care. Five descriptive and qualitative studies suggest that AI oversight is often fragmented or absent, and 77 sources endorse forming such a body.

perspectives.view: None of the five studies compares organizations with and without a governance body, so none tests the practice. All five are level 3 qualitative or survey designs that document the hazard. They show consistent reports of fragmented or missing oversight, but they cannot show that a committee reduces that problem. Certainty about benefit therefore cannot be rated.

In one survey, 66.7% (36/54) of hospitalists used AI in clinical work with no institutional oversight, and 86.1% used it for differential diagnosis. This suggests that unreviewed tools may already be shaping diagnostic decisions. No study shows whether a governance body would catch these uses or the errors that follow from them.

Professionals and innovators in England reported unclear governance as an implementation barrier. Texas focus group participants described insufficient systematic governance for validation, auditing, and clinical use. These reports identify where governance may be needed in workflow. They do not measure how a committee performs, what burden it adds, or whether its decisions are followed in practice.

Among 19 organizations, 78.9% reported using steering committees for AI oversight, and some of these were combined with IT, research, or innovation teams. The authors still found fragmented approaches. This suggests that having a committee may not be enough by itself. The studies report no data on staffing, cost, or which committee structures worked.

Five safety-net organizations named AI governance structures as a key barrier during integration and lifecycle management, and the study reports no numeric results. This indicates that governance capacity may be thinner where resources are limited. No study tests whether a governance body improves equity outcomes for Medicaid, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

One endorsing source cites a federal final rule that requires reasonable efforts to identify and mitigate algorithmic discrimination. A governance body is one way an organization could document those efforts. No supplied study examines whether a governance body helps organizations meet this or any other regulatory obligation.

Patient advocates and patient and public involvement participants took part in two of the qualitative studies, and the participants described unclear or insufficient governance. Neither study reports whether patient members on a governance body changed decisions or affected patients' trust or their ability to reach a human.

commentary.research_gap: The evidence base lacks comparative studies, even before-and-after or multi-site observational designs, that relate the presence, membership, and decision rights of an AI governance body to measurable outcomes. Candidate outcomes include unsanctioned AI use, detected safety events, completed validations, and equity audits. Such studies should also report staffing and cost.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One hazard study drew on five safety-net organizations serving low-income patients and reported governance as a barrier. This suggests that the organizations most likely to lack governance capacity are also the least studied in terms of what helps.
